html:
Timbuktu is a city in Mali on the southern edge of the Sahara, about 20 km north of the Niger River. It began as a seasonal camp of Tuareg herders and became a permanent town early in the 1100s.

It sat where desert met river. Camel caravans of the trans-Saharan trade brought salt from mines in the desert; boats on the Niger brought gold, grain and slaves from the south. The town lived by swapping one for the other.

  • The Mali Empire held it in the 1300s. After Mansa Musa came back from his pilgrimage in the 1320s, the Djinguereber mosque was built, linked to the architect Abu Ishaq es-Sahili.
  • Ibn Battuta passed through in 1353.
  • The Songhai Empire took it in 1468. Under Songhai it reached its height as a centre of Islamic learning, with scholars teaching around the Sankore mosque and families keeping large private libraries, the Timbuktu manuscripts.

A Moroccan army took the city after the Battle of Tondibi in 1591 and deported leading scholars, among them Ahmad Baba, to Marrakesh. As trade moved to the Atlantic coast, the town shrank. In Europe its name came to mean the far end of the earth. In 2012 armed Islamist groups wrecked shrines and burned some manuscripts, but many had been smuggled out to safety.
sum: Timbuktu is a city in Mali on the southern edge of the Sahara, about 20 km north of the Niger River. It began as a seasonal camp of Tuareg herders and became a permanent town early in the 1100s.
